claim: The B.1.1.7 variant is thought to have first emerged in the UK in September 2020.

claim: The B.1.1.7 variant has been detected in over 50 countries.

claim: Sera were collected from 29 patients with confirmed B.1.1.7 infection who were admitted to University College London Hospitals for unrelated reasons.
source: To examine the antibody response to B.1.1.7, we collected sera from 29 patients, admitted to University College London Hospitals (UCLH) for unrelated reasons (Supplementary file 1), who had confirmed B.1.1.7 infection.
evidence: Describes the study design and sample collection

claim: 23 out of 29 B.1.1.7 infected patients displayed relatively mild COVID-19 symptoms.

evidence: Reports observed clinical outcomes in the study cohort

claim: 6 out of 29 B.1.1.7 infected patients remained COVID-19-asymptomatic.

claim: Antibody titres may depend on the severity of SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: As antibody titres may depend on the severity of SARS-CoV-2 infection, as well as on time since infection (Gaebler et al., 2021; Long et al., 2020), we compared B.1.1.7 sera with sera collected during the first wave of D614G variant spread in London from hospitalised COVID-19 patients (Ng et al., 2020) (n=20) and mild/asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2-infected health care workers (Houlihan et al., 2020) (n=17) who were additionally sampled 2 months later.
evidence: Supported by citations to Gaebler et al., 2021 and Long et al., 2020

claim: Antibody titres may depend on time since infection.

claim: Titres of antibodies that bound the parental D614G spike largely correlated with those that bound the B.1.351 spike.

claim: The correlation between antibody binding to D614G and variant spikes is consistent with the high degree of similarity between the spike proteins.

claim: D614G infection appeared to induce substantial cross-neutralisation of the B.1.1.7 variant.

claim: Neutralisation of the parental Wuhan strain by B.1.1.7 sera was significantly reduced compared to neutralisation of the infecting B.1.1.7 variant.
source: However, the reverse was not true. Neutralisation of the parental Wuhan strain by B.1.1.7 sera was significantly reduced, compared to neutralisation of the infecting B.1.1.7 variant (fold change −3.4; range −1.20 to −10.6, p<0.001) (Figure 2b), and the difference in cross-neutralisation drop was also significant (p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 2b

claim: The difference in cross-neutralisation drop between D614G and B.1.1.7 sera was statistically significant (p<0.001).

claim: B.1.1.7 sera displayed significantly reduced neutralisation of the B.1.351 variant with a fold change of −7.7.

claim: B.1.1.7 sera contained higher absolute levels of neutralising antibodies than D614G sera against the infecting variant (p=0.003).

claim: Mutations in SARS-CoV-2 variants B.1.1.7 and B.1.351 reduce recognition by antibodies elicited by natural infection with the D614G variant.
source: Mutations in severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) variants that arose in the United Kingdom (UK) (B.1.1.7; Alpha) or in South Africa (B.1.351; Beta) reduce recognition by antibodies elicited by natural infection with the parental reference (Wuhan) strain and the subsequent D614G variant (Cele et al., 2021; Diamond et al., 2021; Edara et al., 2021; Emary et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021b; Planas et al., 2021; Skelly et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021; Wibmer et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Reduction in cross-reactivity impinges the effectiveness of current vaccines based on the Wuhan strain.
source: Such reduction in cross-reactivity also impinges the effectiveness of current vaccines based on the Wuhan strain (Diamond et al., 2021; Edara et al., 2021; Emary et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021b; Skelly et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2021), prompting consideration of alternative vaccines based on the new variants.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Antibodies elicited by B.1.1.7 infection exhibited significantly reduced recognition of parental strains compared to the infecting variant.
source: Antibodies elicited by B.1.1.7 infection exhibited significantly reduced recognition and neutralisation of parental strains or of the South Africa variant B.1.351 (Beta) than of the infecting variant.
evidence: Main finding from the study data

claim: Heterotypic immunity induced by SARS-CoV-2 variants is asymmetric.
source: The results indicate that heterotypic immunity induced by SARS-CoV-2 variants is asymmetric.
evidence: Main conclusion from the study findings

claim: Sera from D614G infection retained 52% neutralisation of B.1.1.7 in severe infection.
source: However, the stronger heterotypic recognition of B.1.1.7 by D614G sera was independent of severity of infection and was, in fact, more pronounced in mild/asymptomatic than in severe D614G infection, when the two were considered separately, with sera from severe and mild/asymptomatic D614G infection retaining 52% and 85% neutralisation of B.1.1.7 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Sera from mild/asymptomatic D614G infection retained 85% neutralisation of B.1.1.7.
source: However, the stronger heterotypic recognition of B.1.1.7 by D614G sera was independent of severity of infection and was, in fact, more pronounced in mild/asymptomatic than in severe D614G infection, when the two were considered separately, with sera from severe and mild/asymptomatic D614G infection retaining 52% and 85% neutralisation of B.1.1.7 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The ability of sera from mild/asymptomatic D614G to neutralise B.1.1.7 did not change over time.
source: Moreover, the ability of sera from mild/asymptomatic D614G to neutralise B.1.1.7 did not change over time (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by longitudinal data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Binding antibody titres were significantly reduced for all three Ig classes in D614G sera in the 2 months of follow-up.
source: Indeed, whilst binding antibody titres were significantly reduced for all three Ig classes in D614G sera in the 2 months of follow-up, neutralising antibody titres remained comparable for the Wuhan and B.1.1.7 strains and were undetectable at both time-points for the B.1.351 strain (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by longitudinal data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Neutralising antibody titres remained comparable for the Wuhan and B.1.1.7 strains over 2 months in D614G sera.
source: Indeed, whilst binding antibody titres were significantly reduced for all three Ig classes in D614G sera in the 2 months of follow-up, neutralising antibody titres remained comparable for the Wuhan and B.1.1.7 strains and were undetectable at both time-points for the B.1.351 strain (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by longitudinal data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Neutralising antibody titres against B.1.351 were undetectable at both time-points in D614G sera.
source: Indeed, whilst binding antibody titres were significantly reduced for all three Ig classes in D614G sera in the 2 months of follow-up, neutralising antibody titres remained comparable for the Wuhan and B.1.1.7 strains and were undetectable at both time-points for the B.1.351 strain (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by longitudinal data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: In matched subsets, D614G sera retained 87% neutralisation of B.1.1.7.
source: Analysis of these comparable subsets further supported the notion that B.1.1.7 infection elicited reduced heterotypic immunity, with D614G and B.1.1.7 sera retaining 87% and 42% neutralisation of B.1.1.7 and D614G, respectively, and much lower neutralisation of B.1.351 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data from matched samples shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: In matched subsets, B.1.1.7 sera retained 42% neutralisation of D614G.
source: Analysis of these comparable subsets further supported the notion that B.1.1.7 infection elicited reduced heterotypic immunity, with D614G and B.1.1.7 sera retaining 87% and 42% neutralisation of B.1.1.7 and D614G, respectively, and much lower neutralisation of B.1.351 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data from matched samples shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: B.1.1.7 sera contained higher absolute levels of neutralising antibodies than D614G sera against the infecting variant in matched samples.
source: Although analysis of larger numbers of samples will be required to conclusively determine if B.1.1.7 infection is more immunogenic than D614G infection, the current data highlight the effect of the severity of infection on resulting antibody titres and the importance of controlling for such confounding factors.
evidence: Inference from comparison of matched samples

claim: The B.1.351 virus isolate acquired Q677H and R682W mutations at the furin cleavage site during passage in Vero V1 cells.
source: However, sequencing of viral genomes isolated following further passage in Vero V1 cells identified the Q677H and R682W mutations at the furin cleavage site, in approximately 50% of the genomes.
evidence: Observation from viral sequencing after cell culture passage
